questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.learningObjective: Distinguish a research question from a topic
questions.stem: An analyst drafts a dashboard note titled 'stress in nurses'; what would turn it into a research question

options.text: Ask how stress levels differ by shift length among nurses

options.misconception: treats a label as a question

questions.explanation: A research question specifies a measurable relationship or comparison, not just a topic. 'How stress differs by shift length' is answerable and testable. A topic alone lacks variables and direction.
questions.hint: A question needs variables and a comparison.

provenance.author: bank-team-research-methods
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.stem: An analyst writes 'Does training reduce errors?' then adds 'Training reduces errors by 20 percent'; which is the hypothesis

options.text: The first sentence is the hypothesis
The second sentence is the hypothesis

options.misconception: fails to separate question and prediction

questions.explanation: The research question asks whether an effect exists; the hypothesis predicts the direction and size of the effect. The second sentence makes a testable prediction. Questions and predictions serve different roles.

provenance.author: bank-team-research-methods
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.stem: An analyst proposes 'All managers are secretly anxious'; why is this not scientific

options.text: It cannot be tested or refuted

questions.explanation: A scientific claim must be falsifiable, meaning evidence could refute it. 'Secretly anxious' is defined to evade any observation, so no evidence could disprove it. Falsifiability is the demarcation criterion.

provenance.author: bank-team-research-methods
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.stem: An analyst measures 'fatigue' by hours of sleep lost; what is this called
questions.explanation: An operational definition specifies how a concept is measured or manipulated. Hours of sleep lost is a concrete measurement of fatigue. Theoretical definitions describe meaning without measurement.

provenance.author: bank-team-research-methods
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.stem: An analyst tests whether a new training reduces call handling time; which variable is independent
questions.explanation: The independent variable is manipulated: training type. The dependent variable is measured: call handling time. Other variables are covariates or outcomes. Direction of influence determines the role.

provenance.author: bank-team-research-methods
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.stem: An analyst compares trained and untrained teams, but trained teams also have newer software; what is the software
questions.explanation: A confound is an extraneous variable that varies with the independent variable and could explain the outcome. Newer software co-occurs with training, so its effect is tangled with training's effect.

provenance.author: bank-team-research-methods
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.learningObjective: Explain purpose of a control condition
questions.stem: An analyst includes a group receiving no new training; why include it

options.text: To provide a baseline for comparison

questions.explanation: A control condition provides a comparison baseline, isolating the treatment effect. It does not by itself remove confounds or reduce sample size. Randomisation is a separate procedure.

provenance.author: bank-team-research-methods
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.stem: An analyst randomly assigns analysts to training or control; what does this achieve

options.text: It balances confounds across groups on average
It removes the need for a control group

questions.explanation: Randomisation balances confounding variables across groups in expectation, not with certainty. It does not increase sample size or replace a control group. Balance is probabilistic.

provenance.author: bank-team-research-methods
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.stem: An analyst finds improvement in a group given an inert training; what explains it
questions.explanation: Improvement after an inert intervention can arise from participants' expectations, the placebo effect. This is why blinding and placebo controls matter. It is not evidence the treatment works.

provenance.author: bank-team-research-methods
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.stem: An analyst keeps both participants and raters unaware of group assignment; what does this reduce
questions.explanation: Blinding reduces performance bias, where participants change behaviour, and detection bias, where raters interpret outcomes differently. It does not reduce sampling error or required sample size. Random variation remains.
questions.hint: It reduces bias from knowledge of assignment.

provenance.author: bank-team-research-methods
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.stem: An analyst reports a proportion with a margin of error of 3 percent; what does it describe

options.text: The range likely containing the true population value

questions.explanation: The margin of error quantifies uncertainty in a sample estimate, giving a range likely to contain the true population value. It is not the sample size, individual spread, or p-value.

provenance.author: bank-team-research-methods
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.stem: An analyst notes that two random samples from the same population give slightly different means; what is this called
questions.explanation: Sampling error is the natural variation between sample statistics and the population parameter due to chance in selection. It differs from bias, which is systematic, and from measurement error.
questions.hint: It is chance variation from sampling.

provenance.author: bank-team-research-methods
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.stem: An analyst sends 200 surveys and gets 150 back; what is the response rate
questions.explanation: Response rate = 150/200 = 75 percent. It measures participation among those contacted. A low rate threatens representativeness.

provenance.author: bank-team-research-methods
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.stem: An analyst divides a population into subgroups then samples from each; what is this called
questions.explanation: Stratified sampling divides the population into strata and samples from each, ensuring representation. Cluster sampling selects whole groups. Convenience and snowball are non-probability methods.

provenance.author: bank-team-research-methods
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.stem: An analyst randomly selects 10 schools then surveys all students in them; what is this called
questions.explanation: Cluster sampling selects groups (clusters) and includes all or a sample within them. It differs from stratified sampling, which samples from every stratum. It is useful when a full population list is unavailable.

provenance.author: bank-team-research-methods
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.stem: An analyst checks whether two coders agree on rating interview transcripts; what is this called
questions.explanation: Inter-rater reliability measures agreement between different raters or coders. Test-retest measures stability over time. Internal consistency measures item coherence. Validity is about accuracy, not agreement.

provenance.author: bank-team-research-methods
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.topic: Margin of error and sample size
questions.learningObjective: Relate margin of error to sample size
questions.stem: An analyst wants a smaller margin of error without changing confidence; what must change
questions.explanation: Margin of error decreases as sample size increases, roughly with the square root of n. Population size matters little for large populations. Confidence level also affects margin but was held constant.

provenance.author: bank-team-research-methods
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.stem: An analyst finds most participants score the maximum on a knowledge test; what is this called
questions.explanation: A ceiling effect occurs when scores cluster at the maximum, limiting ability to detect improvement. A floor effect is clustering at the minimum. Both restrict range and reduce sensitivity.

provenance.author: bank-team-research-methods
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.stem: An analyst computes required n before collecting data; what inputs are typically needed
questions.explanation: Sample size planning uses the expected effect size, significance level alpha, and desired power. Population size matters little for large populations. Budget and p-values are not planning inputs.

provenance.author: bank-team-research-methods
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.stem: An analyst uses a list of all registered nurses in a region as the sampling frame; what is it

options.text: The list from which the sample is drawn

questions.explanation: The sampling frame is the operational list or source from which the sample is selected. It should match the target population as closely as possible. Gaps cause coverage error.
questions.hint: It is the list you sample from.

provenance.author: bank-team-research-methods
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.stem: An analyst must choose between stratified and cluster sampling for a national survey; which is usually more precise
questions.explanation: Stratified sampling usually reduces variance by ensuring representation across key subgroups. Cluster sampling often increases variance due to within-cluster similarity. Choice depends on cost and logistics.

provenance.author: bank-team-research-methods
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.learningObjective: Identify a cost of cluster sampling
questions.stem: An analyst uses cluster sampling to save money; what trade-off often results

options.text: Higher design effect and wider intervals

questions.explanation: Cluster sampling reduces cost but often increases the design effect, widening confidence intervals for the same n. The savings come at a precision cost. Plan accordingly.

provenance.author: bank-team-research-methods
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.stem: An analyst finds selected participants do not answer; what problem arises
questions.explanation: Nonresponse can bias estimates if nonrespondents differ from respondents. Even random selection does not fix nonresponse bias. Follow-up and weighting can help.

provenance.author: bank-team-research-methods
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.learningObjective: Explain risk of low response rates
questions.stem: An analyst achieves a 15 percent response rate; what is the main concern

options.misconception: confuses low rate with high cost

options.text: No concern if the sample is random

questions.explanation: A low response rate raises the risk that respondents differ systematically from nonrespondents, biasing estimates. Random selection of the initial sample does not prevent this. Weighting and follow-up help.

provenance.author: bank-team-research-methods
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.stem: An analyst records education as 'high school, bachelor, master, doctorate'; what level is this
questions.explanation: Ordered categories with unequal intervals are ordinal. Nominal lacks order. Interval and ratio require equal intervals and, for ratio, a true zero. Education levels are ordered but intervals are not equal.

provenance.author: bank-team-research-methods
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.stem: An analyst's scale gives consistent results but measures the wrong construct; what is it
questions.explanation: Reliability is consistency; validity is measuring the right thing. A scale can be consistent yet measure the wrong construct, so it is reliable but not valid. Validity requires reliability but reliability alone is not enough.

provenance.author: bank-team-research-methods
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.stem: An analyst correlates a new aptitude test with job performance ratings; what validity is this
questions.explanation: Criterion validity evaluates a measure against an external criterion, such as job performance. Content validity checks domain coverage. Construct validity checks theoretical alignment. Face validity is superficial appearance.
questions.hint: It compares against an external criterion.

provenance.author: bank-team-research-methods
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.stem: An analyst checks whether a depression scale relates to sleep and appetite as theory predicts; what validity is this
questions.explanation: Construct validity examines whether a measure behaves as the theoretical construct predicts, including convergent and discriminant patterns. It goes beyond a single external criterion.

provenance.author: bank-team-research-methods
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.stem: An analyst gives the same questionnaire twice two weeks apart and correlates scores; what is this
questions.explanation: Test-retest reliability assesses stability of scores over time. Inter-rater involves different raters. Split-half divides items. Validity concerns accuracy, not stability.

provenance.author: bank-team-research-methods
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.stem: An analyst's survey asks 'How often do you feel sad or tired?'; what is the problem

options.text: It confounds two constructs in one item

questions.explanation: The item mixes sadness and tiredness, so a yes answer is ambiguous. Each item should measure one construct. This is a double-barrelled question.

provenance.author: bank-team-research-methods
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.stem: An analyst asks 'Don't you agree the training was excellent?'; what is the issue
questions.explanation: The question suggests the desired answer, biasing responses. Leading questions push respondents toward agreement. Neutral wording avoids this.

provenance.author: bank-team-research-methods
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.stem: An analyst uses a 5-point scale from 'strongly disagree' to 'strongly agree' with no neutral midpoint; what is the risk

options.text: Forced choice may distort true neutral views

questions.explanation: Removing the neutral midpoint forces respondents to choose a side, which can distort those who are genuinely neutral. This is a forced-choice scale. It may reduce fence-sitting but also loses information.
questions.hint: No neutral option forces a side.

provenance.author: bank-team-research-methods
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.stem: An analyst asks about overall job satisfaction before asking about pay; later responses shift; what is this
questions.explanation: Earlier questions can prime or anchor responses to later ones, creating question order effects. Randomising item order or using funnel sequences can reduce this. It is a measurement issue, not sampling.

provenance.author: bank-team-research-methods
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.stem: An analyst tries a draft questionnaire on 10 people before the main study; what is this called
questions.explanation: Pretesting or piloting checks clarity, timing, and problems before full data collection. It is not randomisation, blinding, or stratification. It improves instrument quality.
questions.hint: It is a small trial run.

provenance.author: bank-team-research-methods
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.stem: An analyst wants to reduce sampling error; which action helps most
questions.explanation: Sampling error decreases with larger sample size. Changing wording affects measurement error, not sampling. Adding variables does not reduce sampling error. Population size has little effect for large populations.

provenance.author: bank-team-research-methods
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.stem: An analyst's frame lists only landline numbers, missing mobile-only households; what error is this
questions.explanation: Coverage error occurs when the frame does not include all members of the target population. Mobile-only households are excluded, biasing estimates. It is a frame problem, not sampling or nonresponse.
questions.hint: The frame misses part of the population.

provenance.author: bank-team-research-methods
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.stem: An analyst builds a scale where each item measures one trait; why does this help

options.text: It improves construct clarity and validity

questions.explanation: Single-construct items improve clarity and construct validity by aligning each item with one trait. It does not guarantee sample size or remove all bias. Length may or may not change.

provenance.author: bank-team-research-methods
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.stem: An analyst defines 'stress' as cortisol level in saliva; what kind of definition is this
questions.explanation: Defining stress as salivary cortisol specifies a measurable procedure, so it is operational. Theoretical definitions describe meaning. Hypotheses predict relationships. Variable type refers to role, not definition.

provenance.author: bank-team-research-methods
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.learningObjective: Identify a confound in a comparison
questions.stem: An analyst compares two departments, but one has more experienced staff; what threatens the comparison
questions.explanation: Experience differs between departments and could explain performance differences, making it a confound. Randomisation or statistical control can address it. Size, reliability, and magnitude are separate issues.

provenance.author: bank-team-research-methods
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.stem: An analyst checks that a math test covers all topics in the syllabus; what validity is this
questions.explanation: Content validity checks whether items adequately cover the domain of interest. Criterion validity uses an external standard. Construct validity tests theory. Face validity is superficial.

provenance.author: bank-team-research-methods
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.learningObjective: Rewrite a topic as a question
questions.stem: An analyst's note says 'remote work productivity'; write a research question that is testable

answer.exemplar: Does remote work productivity differ between employees with a dedicated home office and those without one, measured by weekly output? This question names variables, a comparison, and an outcome, making it testable with data.

questions.explanation: A testable research question names variables, a comparison, and a measurable outcome. The topic alone lacks these. The exemplar shows how to convert a topic into an inquiry.

provenance.author: bank-team-research-methods
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.learningObjective: Write a hypothesis from a question
questions.stem: An analyst asks 'Does sleep affect memory?'; write a testable hypothesis

answer.exemplar: Participants who sleep eight hours will recall more words than those who sleep four hours. The hypothesis predicts direction and groups, unlike the question which only asks whether an effect exists.

questions.explanation: A hypothesis predicts the expected relationship and direction, going beyond the question. It should be specific enough to test with data. The exemplar includes groups and predicted outcome.

provenance.author: bank-team-research-methods
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.stem: An analyst tests 'All swans are white'; what evidence would falsify it
questions.explanation: A universal claim is falsified by a single counterexample. Many confirming cases do not prove it. Redefining terms or polling opinions does not test the claim.

provenance.author: bank-team-research-methods
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.stem: An analyst defines 'happiness' as number of smiles per hour; what limitation should be noted

options.text: It may not capture the full construct

questions.explanation: Smiles are a narrow proxy for happiness and may miss other aspects like life satisfaction. Operational definitions are always partial. Objectivity is a strength, not a flaw.
questions.hint: One proxy may miss the construct.

provenance.author: bank-team-research-methods
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.stem: An analyst studies whether lighting level affects reading speed; which is the dependent variable
questions.explanation: Reading speed is the measured outcome, so it is dependent. Lighting level is manipulated, so it is independent. Temperature and age are covariates to control.

provenance.author: bank-team-research-methods
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.stem: An analyst compares two training methods, but groups differ in prior experience; best control

options.text: Randomise assignment or match on experience

questions.explanation: Randomisation or matching on the confound balances or controls it. Ignoring it leaves bias. Changing dose or removing participants does not address the confound properly.
questions.hint: Randomise or match on the confound.

provenance.author: bank-team-research-methods
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.stem: An analyst tests a new drug; which control condition is most appropriate

options.text: A group from a different population
A group receiving double the dose
A placebo group receiving an inert pill

questions.explanation: A placebo control isolates the treatment effect from expectation and natural change. No control prevents comparison. Different dose or population introduces confounds. Placebo is the standard.

provenance.author: bank-team-research-methods
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.stem: An analyst has 60 participants and wants two groups of 30; best method
questions.explanation: Random assignment balances confounds in expectation. Arrival order or self-selection introduce bias. Stratification by gender is a different design. Simple randomisation is appropriate here.

provenance.author: bank-team-research-methods
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.stem: An analyst wants to separate treatment effect from expectation; what design feature helps
questions.explanation: A placebo control plus blinding separates the treatment's specific effect from expectation. Sample size, extra variables, and population changes do not control for placebo. This is the standard approach.

provenance.author: bank-team-research-methods
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.stem: An analyst's outcome is subjective ratings; which blinding is most important
questions.explanation: Subjective ratings are vulnerable to detection bias, so raters must be blinded. Participant blinding also helps. Blinding only the statistician does not prevent rating bias. Double-blind is best.

provenance.author: bank-team-research-methods
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.stem: An analyst estimates a proportion 0.50 from n=100 with z=1.96; margin of error as decimal
questions.explanation: MOE = z times sqrt(p(1-p)/n) = 1.96 times sqrt(0.25/100) = 1.96 times 0.05 = 0.098. This assumes simple random sampling. Larger n reduces MOE.

provenance.author: bank-team-research-methods
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.stem: An analyst has sample mean 50, population sd 10, n=25; standard error of the mean
questions.explanation: SEM = sigma over sqrt(n) = 10 over 5 = 2. This measures variability of the sample mean. Larger n reduces SEM. It is not the standard deviation of individuals.

provenance.author: bank-team-research-methods
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.stem: An analyst sends 400 surveys and receives 260 complete; response rate as percent
questions.explanation: Response rate = 260/400 times 100 = 65 percent. Only complete responses count if that is the definition. Report the denominator clearly.

provenance.author: bank-team-research-methods
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.stem: An analyst stratifies by department of sizes 300 and 700, total n=100; proportional allocation to smaller stratum
questions.explanation: Smaller stratum share = 300/1000 = 0.3, so sample = 0.3 times 100 = 30. Proportional allocation mirrors population shares. Larger stratum gets 70.

provenance.author: bank-team-research-methods
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.stem: An analyst needs 120 participants, each cluster has 15 people; how many clusters needed
questions.explanation: Clusters needed = 120/15 = 8. This assumes no partial clusters and full participation. Real studies add extra clusters for attrition.
questions.hint: Divide total n by cluster size.

provenance.author: bank-team-research-methods
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.stem: An analyst reports 85 percent agreement between two coders; what does this suggest
questions.explanation: 85 percent agreement indicates good but not perfect inter-rater reliability. Perfect would be 100 percent. Reliability does not establish validity. Consider chance-corrected metrics like kappa.

provenance.author: bank-team-research-methods
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.topic: Margin of error and sample size
questions.learningObjective: Compute required n for target MOE
questions.stem: An analyst wants MOE 0.05 for p=0.5 at z=1.96; required n (rounded up)
questions.explanation: n = (z^2 p(1-p))/MOE^2 = (1.96^2 times 0.25)/0.0025 = 384.16, rounded up to 385. This is the standard formula for proportions. Larger MOE needs smaller n.

provenance.author: bank-team-research-methods
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.learningObjective: Identify a ceiling effect in data
questions.stem: An analyst sees 40 percent of participants at the maximum score; what does this indicate
questions.explanation: Clustering at the maximum indicates a ceiling effect, which can hide differences and improvements. It is not perfect performance by all, since only 40 percent hit the max. A floor effect would cluster at the minimum.
questions.hint: Clustering at max is a ceiling effect.

provenance.author: bank-team-research-methods
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.stem: An analyst's power analysis recommends n=120 for 80 percent power; what if only 80 are recruited
questions.explanation: Power depends on sample size; recruiting fewer than planned reduces power below the target. This increases risk of a false negative. Re-run the analysis for the actual n.

provenance.author: bank-team-research-methods
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.stem: An analyst uses an alumni email list to study current students; what is the problem

options.text: The frame does not match the target population

questions.explanation: An alumni list excludes current students not in it and includes non-students, causing coverage error. The frame must match the target population. This is a common frame mismatch.

provenance.author: bank-team-research-methods
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used
